senses.gloss:
Sūryanārāyaṇa
------------------------------------------
Sūrya, the Sun-god, is said to be pervaded by विष्णु or नारायण in his aspect as त्रिविक्रम. He is a Vedic deity. He is invoked in the solar orb at the time of the सन्ध्या ritual. He is visualised as seated on a lotus-seat and is of golden colour. He has a beautiful crown on his head, armlets and ear-rings in the form of makaras (crocodiles) and holds the शङ्ख (conch) and चक्र (discus) in his hands.

Sūrdās
(A. D. 1471-1584)
------------------------------------------
One of the greatest saints and poets of Hindi devotional literature, सूर्दास् has etched for himself an indelible place in the cult of Kṛṣṇabhakti or devotion to कृष्ण. Born blind in a ब्राह्मण family of the village of Sihi near Delhi, he was, yet, endowed with extraordinary powers of perception. It was perhaps this power that made him, in his later life, have visions of कृष्ण in his heart. He also had a prodigious memory that helped him to memorise the whole of the Bhāgavata- purāṇa and several devotional texts.
SūrdāsNeglected by his parents and even ill-treated by them sometimes, he left his home and started living on the bank of the river यमुना at a place called Gaughāṭ.
The turning point in his life came when he received initiation from Vallabhā-cārya (A. D. 1473-1531), the great teacher of puṣṭimārga (See PUṢṬIMĀRGA.). After this he is said to have lived in Govardhan near मथुरा (in Uttar Pradesh).
Vallabha inspired him to devote himself to the portrayal of कृष्ण’s playful moods as also the incidents depicted in the folklore on कृष्ण.
Sūrdās is said to have composed 100,000 songs of which only 8000 are available today. They have been brought out in a book form known as Sūrsāgar (ocean of सूर्दास् songs). The songs are written in Brajbhāṣā, a Hindi dialect of the मथुरा region. They are highly musical and extremely popular. The themes are always centred round कृष्ण whether pertaining to his childish pranks or the रासलीला, his famous dance with the गोपीस् of वृन्दाबन्.

Śūrpaṇakhā
(‘one whose nails resembled a winnowing basket’)
------------------------------------------
Śūrpaṇakhā is one of the two iniquitous ladies—the other being Mantharā—but for whom the classic, the Rāmāyaṇa, would never have been composed, thereby depriving millions of people for millenniums, of the great inspiration for life!
She was the daughter of the sage Viśravas and Kaikasī. She was younger than रावण and कुम्भकर्ण but older than विभीषण. She had been married to Vidyujjihva who was killed by रावण since he had joined the enemy camp. As a result of her pleadings, रावण made arrangements for her stay in the दण्डक forest with Khara and Dūṣana, with their large army to protect her.
Infatuated with Rāmā’s beauty, she pressed him to marry her, abandoning सीता. When she tried to kill सीता, राम got her punished through लक्ष्मण who cut off her nose and ears.
Her complaints to Khara and रावण resulted in the decimation of Khara and his army at the hands of राम, and the abduction of सीता by रावण.

Sūrya
(‘Sun-god’)
------------------------------------------
Sūrya or the sun, often identified with आदित्य, Savitṛ and पूषन्, is an important Vedic deity. He is extremely brilliant and rides in an exquisitely beautiful chariot drawn by seven horses. He is compared to a bird that flies in the sky and is described as the jewel of the sky. He gives light, produces day and night, gives power and strength to the living beings, makes them active, and destroys their laziness and disease.
Savitṛ is the aspect of the sun before sunrise. He is golden all over. He establishes people in their respective places. He gives life and energy and guides people in the right path.
The famous Gāyatrīmantra is dedicated to this Savitṛ.
The nourishing and life-supporting aspect of the sun is personified and praised as पूषन्. He is exceedingly beautiful. He destroys the evil ones with the discus he wears. He looks upon all with an equal eye. He is extremely generous and ever ready to protect.
The story of सूर्य appears in many of the पुराणस् as also the two epics.
He was the son of कश्यप and अदिति. Saṁjñādevī, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, was his wife. यम and मनु were his sons whereas यमुना was his daughter. Sāvarṇa and Śanaiścara were his sons born to Chāyādevī (a replica of सṁज्ञा-देवी). The अश्विन्स् were also his sons born to सṁज्ञा when she had assumed the form of a mare.
It was by his blessings that कुन्ती (the मोथेर् of the Pāṇḍavas) gave birth to कर्ण (See KARṆA for details.)
Aruṇa was his charioteer.
When the Pāṇḍavas had been banished to the forest, युधिष्ठिर appeased सूर्य by an earnest prayer and received from him, the अक्षयपात्र (a vessel that was always filled with delicious ड़ोओद्).
It was he who bestowed the Śukla Yajurveda on the sage याज्ञवल्क्य at his earnest prayer.
Agastya taught राम, the Ādityahṛdayastotra in praise of सूर्य, by repeating which he was able to kill रावण.
Sūrya is also included in the list of नवग्रहस् or Nine प्लनेत्स्. He is the first of the nine ग्रहस्. He rides on a chariot with one wheel and seven horses with अरुण, the Red one, as his charioteer. Almost all temples have the images of the नवग्रहस् in their vicinity with सूर्य in the centre.
See also ĀDITYA.

suras
(‘gods’)
------------------------------------------
The words sura and asura are commonly used in the Vedic and paurāṇic literature. They stand for the gods and the antigods or demons.
Sura is one of the 25 names of the gods.
The word asura is sometimes defined as one who revels in his senses (sveṣu asuṣu ramaṇāt). That means, the persons given to reckless sense-enjoyments. As opposed to them are the सुरस्, the divine beings, beings of light and wisdom.
See ASURAS and DEVAS.

surāpāna
(‘consuming intoxicating drinks’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu scriptures have always condemned सुरापान or मद्यपान, consuming of intoxicating drinks as mahāpātaka or a grave sin (vide Chandogya Upaniṣad 5.10.9; Manusmṛti 11.54; Āpastamba Dharmasūtras 1.7.21.8).
Surā is the intoxicating drink prepared out of flour. (It should not be confused with the सोम juice). Other drinks like the ones prepared out of molasses or madhūka flowers were permitted to be taken by the kṣattriyas and vaiśyas. But, the ब्राह्मणस् were strictly forbidden from consuming all types of intoxicants.
It is interesting to note that surā was one of the oblations made in the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice.

Sureśvara
------------------------------------------
Sureśvara was one of the four chief disciples of शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820). Not much is known about him.
According to the traditional bio-graphies of Śaṅkara—like the Śaṅkara-digvijaya—he was मण्डन मिश्र, a great scholar of Mīmāṁsā, whom शङ्कर defeated in a disputation. As per the earlier agreement, he accepted सṁन्यास from शङ्कर and became his disciple, assuming the new name सुरेश्वर. Modern scholars however do not subscribe to this view. According to them he was an entirely different person, known earlier as विश्वरूप.
Sureśvara’s works are Vārttikas (poetical expositions) on शङ्कर’s bhāṣyas (commentaries) on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the Taittirīya Upaniṣads; Mānasollāsa a (vārttika) on the Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra; a bhāṣya on शङ्कर’s Pañcīkaraṇa; Naiṣkarmyasiddhi (an independent treatise on Advaita Vedānta).
He was the first pontiff of the Śāradāpīṭha of Śṛṅgerī, one of the four monasteries established by शङ्कर.
According to another version, he was the first pontiff of the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi-pīṭham (after शङ्कर), a fifth monastery supposed to have been established by शङ्कर himself for his own stay. The controversy regarding this point is still very much alive. It is however true that this मठ also has produced many great ācāryas.

Śūrasena
------------------------------------------
Śūrasena was the name of a जनपद or a country, one of the sixteen well-known janapadas that existed during the time of Mahābhārata. It was probably established by the king Śūra, the ड़थेर् of Vasudeva and कुन्ती. Its capital was मथुरा.

Sūryagītā
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor Gītās composed in imitation of the well-known Bhagavadgītā. It forms a part of a bigger work, Gurujñāna-vāsiṣṭha-tattvasārāyaṇa.
It is spread over five chapters and has 376 verses. It is in the form of a dialogue between the charioteer अरुण and his master सूर्य.
The philosophy is Śivādvaita, advaita centred round शिव.
Mukti is attained by the combined practice of ज्ञान (knowledge), कर्म (action, rituals) and upāsanā (meditation). For a sādhaka (spiritual aspirant) all the three are equally important.
There is a nice description of the eternal attributes (nityavibhūtis) and the playful attributes (līlāvibhūtis) of शिव followed by the attributes of a perfected सोउल्, called karmiśreṣṭha. These are similar to those of the स्थितप्रज्ञ in the Bhagavadgītā (2.55-72).

sūryabhedana
------------------------------------------
Works on the हठयोग describe eight kinds of कुम्भक, the second of the three steps of प्राणायाम (Gheraṇḍa-saṁhitā 5.46 onwards; Haṭhayoga-pradīpikā 2.44).
Out of these the सूर्यभेदन is also one. The air that is inhaled through the right nostril, after closing the left nostril, should be retained until one feels that it fills up to the tip of nails and hair. This is called सूर्यभेदन. It destroys disorders of wind (vāta) as also worms.
The technique has to be learnt from experts in the field.

Sūryakuṇḍa
(‘lake of the Sun’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu places of पिल्ग्रिमगे are legion in India.
About 8 kms. (5 miles) away from अयोध्या (in Uttar Pradesh) is situated the सूर्यकुण्ड. It is a fairly large lake with steps on all the four sides for devotees who want to take bath. On its western side is a temple dedicated to the god सूर्यनारायण.

Sūryasiddhānta
------------------------------------------
Hindu अस्त्रोनोम्य् is a very ancient science. Its source-book is the Sūrya-siddhānta. It was taught by सूर्य (Sun-god) to मय (the architect of the असुरस्) at the end of the कृतयुग.
The work that is available now might have taken shape during A. D. 400. वराहमिहिर (A. D. 550) made use of this work in his Pañcasiddhāntikā. It has three commentaries, the authors being Kamalā-kara (A. D. 1616), परमेश्वर (A. D. 1360-1455) and रङ्गनाथ (A. D. 1640). Of these, the last one is the most detailed.
The book is divided into 14 chapters.
The following is a brief summary of its contents:
Chapter 1
It deals with the mean motion of the प्लनेत्स्. It also gives enough information to calculate the mean daily motion of the प्लनेत्स्.
Chapter 2
The method of calculating the true position of a planet including the corrections needed for its retrograde motion is given here.
Chapter 3
This chapter deals with direction, place and time. The method of constructing a sun-dial is also given.
Chapter 4
Both the eclipses—especially the lunar eclipse—are dealt with here.
Chapter 5
Calculations for the parallax of the solar एच्लिप्से are given here.
Chapter 6
This describes the manner of exhibiting by a projection, the various phases of an एच्लिप्से.
Chapter 7
Planetary conjunctions are the subject dealt with here.
Chapter 8
This chapter gives the positions of the various nakṣatras (or groups of स्तर्स्).
Chapter 9
Heliacal rising and setting of the प्लनेत्स् are described here.
Chapter 10
This gives the calculations needed to correctly state the rising and setting of the मोओन्.
Chapter 11
This is partly astrological in nature. The malignant character of the time as related to the sun and the मोओन् is given here along with the necessary rules for calculating it.
Chapter 12
The theory of च्रेअतिओन् of the world is the subject-matter of this section.
Chapter 13
This deals with certain instruments needed for the determination of time.
Chapter 14
Different modes of measuring time—solar, sidereal, civil or lunar—are described here.
The text available at present has undergone several corrections over the centuries, the last one being in A. D. 1500.
The trigonometric function of sine is found in this work.
